Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:

  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until

# ARC diagonal-pair ray extension

## When to Use
Use when demonstrations show repeated colors arranged as diagonal neighboring pairs, sometimes among unrelated motifs.

## Rule
Identify same-color cells at `(r,c)` and `(r+1,c±1)`. A qualifying pair indicates that its diagonal line continues through background cells. Extend outward from each endpoint along that same diagonal, coloring only empty/background cells with the pair's color, stopping at a grid boundary or the first non-background cell. Preserve all existing marks and unrelated cells. If one continuation is blocked, the opposite direction may still extend.

## Evidence and validation
- Compare complete input/output deltas before applying the pattern; pairs can be present but produce no new cells when their continuation is already blocked or lies outside the grid.
- Do not extend horizontal or vertical pairs based on this rule.
- For pair `(r,c),(r+1,c-1)`, the diagonal line runs up-right/down-left; for `(r,c),(r+1,c+1)`, it runs up-left/down-right.
- Examples may contain multiple independent pair colors/rays. Apply each evidenced pair separately and preserve original cells.
- Mechanically validate dimensions and replay the inferred operation against every demo, including unchanged cases.

## Continual-ARC observed instance

A same-ID variant, `task-c1bb6949`, had a 10x25 test with background 8 and an unrelated mixed-color 2x2 motif at rows 0-1, columns 9-10: `[3,1;2,5]`. The motif was preserved and the correct output equaled the input. No same-color diagonal-neighbor pair was present, so do not transform salient mixed-color blocks absent the rule's pair trigger. Another confirmed instance had a 9x6 test with background 8 and motif `[0,3;5,6]` at rows 3-4, columns 1-2; it had no same-color diagonal-neighbor pair, so the correct output was unchanged. Its demo contained a 4 pair at `(1,1),(2,2)` (zero-based), which extended southeast along that diagonal. A tempting but incorrect guess extended the lone 6 at `(4,2)` in the test: require the demonstrated equal-color diagonal pair trigger, not an arbitrary colored singleton.
Task `task-c1bb6949` demonstrated this behavior. Find same-color diagonal-neighbor pairs and extend the corresponding diagonal line outward from each endpoint through background cells, stopping at a boundary or the first non-background cell. A blocked side does not prevent the opposite side from extending. Preserve all original cells and unrelated colors. Demo: 7s at `(13,9),(14,10)` extend along the down-right diagonal; 6s at `(13,12),(14,11)` extend up-right from the upper endpoint, while the opposite continuation is blocked by a 7; pair cells are retained. For its test, pairs were 9 at `(8,3),(9,4)`, 6 at `(8,6),(9,5)`, and 7 at `(10,4),(11,3)` (zero-based), and applying the rule solved it. Important payload pitfall: an earlier manually transcribed submission was rejected as an invalid grid because a row had the wrong width. Generate/serialize the whole grid mechanically and verify exactly 18 rows of 22 cells in that test before submitting. Re-derive the rule and dimensions from fresh evidence in recurring variants.

Another validated variant, `task-c1bb6949`, used a 14x13 grid with background 7 and four diagonal pairs: 6 at zero-based `(9,5),(10,6)`, 3 at `(9,8),(10,7)`, 0 at `(11,6),(12,5)`, and 8 at `(11,7),(12,8)`. Extend each pair's diagonal rays through 7s, preserving existing marks and stopping at bounds/non-background. The 6 pair extends to the upper-left boundary from `(9,5)` and down-right to the bottom edge from `(10,6)`. The 3 pair extends up-right from `(9,8)` to the right edge; its opposite ray is blocked by 0 at `(11,6)`. The 0 pair extends down-left from `(12,5)` to `(13,4)`; its opposite ray is blocked by 8 at `(11,7)`. The 8 pair extends down-right from `(12,8)` to `(13,9)`; its opposite ray is blocked by 6 at `(10,6)`. This rule solved the test on the first submission; generated output was mechanically checked as 14 rows × 13 columns.

A second validated instance, `task-c1bb6949`, used a 17x14 grid with background 6. # Connect aligned markers with a bridge color

## When to Use
Use when the input has a uniform background and sparse marker cells, and demonstrations show a third color appearing between aligned markers.

1. Compare input/output cell-by-cell. Confirm original markers stay intact, background stays unchanged outside bridges, and the new color fills only cells between markers sharing a row or column.
2. Determine whether bridges link consecutive markers per row/column or the full span between extreme markers. If all intermediate cells are either markers or filled, these rules are equivalent; test examples with multiple markers.
3. Construct from a copy of the input. For each row, sort marker columns and fill background cells strictly between each consecutive pair with the bridge color. Repeat for each column using sorted marker rows. Keep marker cells unchanged and do not fill beyond the outermost markers.
4. Validate against every demonstration exactly before applying the same operation to the test. Check overlaps where horizontal and vertical bridges meet; they should yield the same bridge color.
5. Validate height, width, and allowed integer colors before submission. Serialize mechanically to avoid row-length/transcription errors; in interactive ARC streams, output exactly one JSON action on the final line.

## Demonstrated pattern

Demonstrated palettes include background 2 / marker 5 / bridge 3, and background 9 with marker 0 or 6 / bridge 3. A 27×28 sparse test with background 9 and marker 6 was solved by preserving markers and filling only intervening cells between consecutive markers in shared rows and columns. Infer palette roles from each task's demos rather than assuming fixed marker/background values.

## Pitfall

A previous answer had the correct intended bridging operation but was rejected as an invalid ARC grid, likely due to a manually copied row-width issue. # Edge-bar / interior-marker beam puzzles

Use when a grid has contiguous color segments on borders plus sparse interior markers, and outputs add aligned rays/stripes and may recolor markers.

## Caution learned from task-d5f2b263

This family can be deceptive: do not assume every isolated marker casts a horizontal/vertical ray, that rays extend toward a nearest edge bar, that bars encode output direction, or that all markers behave alike. These assumptions led to repeated rejected outputs on a task with eight diverse demos. The 5x17 test was not solved; no speculative rule was validated across complete demo pairs.

Demos may involve border runs on opposite sides, runs differing in color from interior markers, markers becoming color 4, marker-associated beams, selected rows/columns, multiple colors, asymmetric edge-defined fills, and altered source cells.

Maintain an exact per-demo delta ledger: record all changed and unchanged cells. Define candidate rules precisely (source markers, direction, color, stop/overwrite behavior, edge interaction, recoloring), then require exact reproduction of every full demo output before applying a rule to test. Explaining conspicuous stripes alone is insufficient.

## Corrected task-2f88c9e9 pattern: parallel stripe before object (coordinate-negative side)

A prior note incorrectly said the stripe is always on the side away from the color-2 bar; that prediction was rejected on the horizontal-bar test. In the demonstrated task-2f88c9e9 subfamily, a full straight color-2 bar and a nearby non-background object are parallel. The demonstrated stripe is a full-grid-length color-8 line parallel to the bar, immediately before the object's extent in grid coordinate order: to the left of a vertical object, or above a horizontal object. Preserve object and source bar. Demo 1: full-height 2-bar at column 5, object at columns 3–4, output full-height 8 stripe at column 2. Demo 2: full-height 2-bar at column 23, broad object around columns 13–21, output full-height 8 stripe at the object's left boundary/preceding column (verify exact edge by full transcription). Demo 3: horizontal 2-bar at row 13, color-5 object in rows 8–10, output full-width 8 stripe at row 9 (the row immediately before the object's top edge; zero-based row 8 in output). Test was solved after rejecting (a) stripe below object and (b) stripe overwriting the object's lower row; accepted output added only a full-width color-8 stripe at zero-based row 4, immediately above the color-6 rows 5–6, while preserving the top color-2 bar and every input cell. Do not infer side from 'away from bar'; use demos to establish coordinate direction and exact object boundary. This is a task-specific validated pattern, not universal.

## Additional evidence: task-d5f2b263 fresh 14×18 instance (unresolved)

A new instance under this ID supplied eight demonstrations, and all eight attempted test outputs were rejected. Do not transfer the earlier accepted 6×24 result above: this is not enough to infer the rule. The demos are heterogeneous and likely expose multiple conditional effects. Key exact deltas/patterns:

- Demo 1 (16×21, bg 7): input has a single 1 at (0,1), vertical 2-run on right edge rows 0–4, vertical 2-run on left edge rows 11–15, and a 2-run at bottom row cols 0–1. Output preserves those 2s, turns (0,1)→4, fills top row cols 2–19 with 1, and fills row 11 cols 1–20 with 1. Other cells unchanged.
- Demo 2 (10×24, bg 7): left edge 8-run rows 0–1, right edge 8-run rows 8–9; marker 0 at (8,4). Output fills top row cols 1–23 with 0, row 8 cols 5–22 with 0, recolors marker (8,4)→4; other cells unchanged.
- Demo 3 (17×6, bg 8): top edge 2-pair at cols 4–5, bottom edge 2-pair cols 2–3, marker 5 at (9,2). Output grows a vertical 5 line down col 4, rows 1–16 (leaving top edge 2s), recolors (9,2)→4, and fills col 2 with 5 for rows 10–15. Bottom edge 2s preserved.
- Demo 4 (23×10, bg 9): left-edge 5 run rows 7–14, right-edge 5 run rows 15–22, markers 3 at (9,8),(11,4). Output adds horizontal 3 fills at row 9 cols 1–7 and row 11 cols 1–3; marker cells become 4. Also rows 17 and 19 get 3 in cols 0–8, preserving right-edge 5s. Other cells unchanged.
- Demo 5 (17×22, bg 6): top-edge 3-run cols 5–8, bottom-edge 3-run cols 18–21, interior 8-pair at row 9 cols 6–7. Output adds vertical 8 stripe rows 0–8 and 10–16 at cols 6–7; the original pair becomes 4s. Edge 3-runs remain intact.
- Demo 6 (25×15, bg 0): right-edge 1 run rows 0–4, left-edge 1 run rows 18–22; 7 markers at (18,11),(19,11),(20,7),(21,4). Output fills rows 0–3 cols 0–13 with 7 (not row 4), fills rows 18–19 cols 1–10 with 7, and row 20 cols 1–6 and row 21 cols 1–3 with 7; each 7 marker becomes 4. Edge 1s preserved.
- Demo 7 (13×21, bg 2): top-edge 9-run cols 7–12 and bottom-edge 9-run cols 15–20; isolated 1s at (2,7),(10,9). Output creates vertical alternating 1 stripes at col 7 (rows 1–2, marker→4, then rows 3–10 as shown), and at cols 15 and 17 (rows 0–11); second marker (10,9)→4 with no obvious adjacent ray. Edges preserved.
- Demo 8 (5×14, bg 6): top-left 7-run cols 0–2, inner 3-pair at row 1 cols 4–5, bottom 7-run cols 3–5. Output fills a vertical 3 stripe at cols 1–2 rows 1–4 and recolors the seed 3s at (1,4–5)→4; it also fills 3 at cols 4–5 rows 2–3, preserving the bottom 7-run. Do not infer a single generic “all runs cast a ray” rule from this.

The rejected guesses for the fresh 14×18 test repeatedly applied a 5-color vertical beam at col 16 and/or 5s down from the two interior markers (5s→4), and one variant used marker cross/fill. Every such submission was incorrect; the actual source-selection/orientation/stop rule remained undetermined after the demo cap. Future recurrence: parse complete input anew, identify source bars and same-color interior motifs, then derive exact per-demo direction/selection, especially run positions and whether rays are gaps/alternating columns. Do not repeat these failed outputs or guess the test merely from the conspicuous color-2 pairs.

## Recovery after rejection

- Whole-grid INCORRECT does not localize the error; do not make arbitrary color or cell edits.
- If feedback says invalid ARC grid, investigate row widths and serialization, not semantics.
- Check height, every row width, integer values 0–9, and JSON parse-roundtrip for the exact payload.
- When demos are exhausted, do not cycle through unvalidated beam directions/colors/extents. Treat each rejected candidate rule as disproven.

## Additional evidence: task-d5f2b263 28×24 instance (unsolved; 8 demos and 8 attempts)

A further instance under this task ID was unsolved. Test input was 28×24, background 7, color-5 border bars at right edge rows 2–8 and left edge rows 21–27, and isolated color-3 markers at zero-based (2,11), (3,4), (5,9), (7,14), (8,6). All eight demos were already used. Eight submissions failed. Failed outputs included broad 3 fills spanning rows 2–8 and 21–27 (with marker cells changed to 4), as well as preserving only bars and changing markers to 4. Do not reuse these guesses. Demos had the same heterogeneous edge-bar/marker behaviors described above; exact full demo deltas were not captured in this conversation context. This instance reinforces that neither filling rows associated with bars nor simply recoloring isolated 3 markers is a validated rule. With no demos/attempts left, the actual rule remains unresolved.

## Additional evidence: task-d5f2b263 (confirmed test)

This task ID has eight heterogeneous demos with changing palettes, edge-run orientations, sparse marker layouts, and line-filling effects. Do not collapse the demos into a universal “every edge run emits rays” or “every marker emits a cross” rule: both failed whole-grid submissions on the confirmed 6×24 test. Demos show that edge-selected fill lines can stop at markers, marker cells can become 4, and different examples use different fill colors and directions; the complete selection predicate is not safely summarized by a single simple rule.

Confirmed test (6×24): background 2; color-1 run on top row, columns 0–6; color-1 run on bottom row, columns 13–19; zero markers at (2,18) and (3,14), zero-based. Correct output preserved both edge runs and the two marker locations as 4, and changed only columns 1, 3, and 5 in rows 1–4 from 2 to 0. All remaining cells were unchanged. This exact result was accepted. Treat it as a task-specific confirmed case, not proof of a general projection rule. In particular, two plausible guesses that added stripes at alternate columns or extended beams from the markers were rejected; after rejection, avoid incremental stripe guessing and use the remaining demos to constrain the complete rule.

## Additional evidence: task-d5f2b263 25×16 test (unresolved; 8 requests, 8 failed submissions)

A separate instance with this ID had test dimensions 25×16, background 5, and sparse 6 markers, with color-2 runs on top and bottom borders. Test input (0-indexed features): top row cols 3–8 are 2 (surrounded by 5); bottom row cols 10–15 are 2; 6s at (6,7), (15,8), and adjacent pair (21,5),(21,6). All other cells are 5. Eight demos were requested and no output was accepted; this is important evidence that the task ID alone does not imply the other saved instance's rule.

Demo 1 (24×17): background 2; 8-runs top row cols 0–6 and bottom row cols 7–13; isolated 0 markers at (10,12),(15,10),(20,13). Output made marker cells 4 and produced distinct horizontal/vertical stripe segments: rows 1–23 at cols 3,5,6 are 0 (with marker/edge interactions), rows 11–23 at col 12 are 0 with marker at (10,12) becoming 4; rows 16–23 at col 10 are 0 with (15,10)→4; row 21 cols 13–14 and row 22 cols 13–14 are 0 with (20,13)→4. Top/bottom 8 edge-runs stay. This is not a simple all-markers-rays result.

Demo 2 (6×29): background 3; top 1-run cols 16–24 and bottom 1-run cols 0–8. Interior 7 cells at (2,20),(2,21),(3,19),(2,24). Output fills row 0 cols 3–5 and col 8 with 7; row 1 cols 3–5 and col 8, and row 1 cols 19–21 and 24 with 7; marker locations shown in output as 4 where applicable; at row 2 cols 20,21,24 markers become 4 and row 2 receives 7 in cols 19 and 23? Exact output should be consulted from transcript when available. Row 3 col 19 becomes 4. Edge runs are preserved. This pair has a left-side separate 7 motif and right markers with local changes, indicating multiple interacting lines.

Demo 3 (24×29): background 0; left edge 7 rows 7–11 and right edge 7 rows 19–23; isolated 6s at (7,14),(9,21),(10,22),(11,10). Output makes 6-filled rectangular/line regions across left spans: row 7 cols 1–13, rows 9–10 cols 1–21, row 11 cols 1–9, with markers changed to 4; right-edge 7s remain and rows 19,21–23 become mostly 6 as displayed. Changes not explained by a simple common beam rule.

Demo 4 (22×29): background 5; top 6 run cols 5–13 and bottom 6 run cols 20–28; isolated 0s at (8,8),(14,13),(17,10). Output puts 0 periodic columns 8,10,13 throughout upper area and cols 23,25,28 across the height; markers become 4 at their positions; run edges preserved. The periodic columns and different marker effects are unlike a uniform all-marker projection.

Demo 5 (14×6): background 0; right-edge 8 rows 8–10; left-edge 8 rows 11–13; 3 markers at (9,3),(10,1). Output changes markers to 4 and fills 3 across row 12 cols 1–5 and row 13 cols 1–5, also local 3s around marker rows: row 9 col 4 gets 3, row 10 cols 2–5 get 3; edge 8s remain.

Demo 6 (30×8): background 8; right edge 3 rows 0–10; left edge 3 rows 11–21; interior 5 markers at (11,6),(12,6),(13,6),(14,5),(15,4),(16,6),(17,6),(18,4),(19,5),(20,5),(21,2). Output recolors the large background region above to 5 (rows 0–10 cols 0–6), preserves 3 borders, and changes each interior 5 marker to 4. The marker's diagonal/adjacent associated pattern turns 5→4 at marked cells and 8→8/5 in directional tails per exact geometry shown in the demo; large area below unchanged. This suggests a distinct regime and cautions against assuming every output only alters markers.

Demo 7 (16×25): background 3; top-left 0 segment cols 0–8 and bottom 0 segment cols 10–18; scattered 2 markers. Output fills a 2-colored periodic horizontal block in cols 0–5 and 7–8 across rows 1–14 (col 6 remains 3); markers are 4 at scattered positions, with vertical 2 patterns at selected columns 10,12,15,17,18 and deviations around markers. Edges preserved. Output seems tied to line/periodic pattern interactions, not straightforward rays.

Demo 8 (8×5): background 8; top row cols 2–3 are 0; bottom row cols 0–1 are 0; one 6 at (6,3). Output paints column 1 rows 0–6 with 6 except top/bottom endpoints, paints column 3 rows 1–5 with 6, changes seed (6,3) to 4; boundary 0 cells remain. Distinct from demos with horizontal fills.

Failed test submissions (all incorrect; 8 attempts ultimately exhausted):
- Repeated first guess: painted 6-filled rectangles/columns in regions derived from markers, changed the three 6 seed/group cells to 4 (except seed patterns varied), plus 6 columns; exact payload is in session record. Rejected.
- Then tried only painting cols 5–8 with 6 from rows 1–20 and 4 at seed cells (6,7),(15,8),(21,5),(21,6); rejected.
- Tried all cells in cols 5–8 of rows 1–20 set to 6, with marker 4s and preserved some bg at rows 7 onward/col distinctions; rejected.
- Tried periodic right-side columns 12–15 in addition to col 5–8 treatment; rejected.
- Tried vertical 6 beams only in cols 5–6 with selected marker changes, and variants with differing starts/stops; all rejected. These were speculative rather than demo-validated and must not be recycled.

Key lesson: eight examples are morphologically heterogeneous and likely encode a richer relation combining border bars, palette, marker positions, and periodic/shape geometry. The task instance remains unresolved. Do not infer merely 'markers cast rays', 'fill edge-associated rectangle', or 'paint every matching column'. # Continual ARC demo inference

Use for interactive ARC tasks where demonstrations arrive incrementally and every request/submission has a cost.

## Protocol and evidence discipline
1. At each turn, note task ID, available demos, used/remaining demo and attempt budgets, and accepted action schema. If the task requires an action JSON only, output exactly one valid JSON object as the final line with no surrounding prose.
2. Keep a compact ledger: for each demo, note input/output shape, recurring structure, exceptional cells, predicted transformation, and any counterexample. Reconstruct rules from all demos, not task-family memory alone.
3. Request another demo only if likely to distinguish specific competing hypotheses. Avoid requests by inertia.
4. Before submitting, formulate a rule that reproduces every demo exactly. Generate the test output mechanically or with carefully indexed coordinates and validate dimensions, row widths, palette range, and serialization.
5. Incorrect feedback is global evidence: reject the full candidate hypothesis. Do not recycle an identical output or make near-identical submissions changing only a few cells without deriving that change from demo evidence. Re-audit the mapping, palette roles, phase, dimensions, and output encoding.

## Exceptional separator-lattice signatures
Some inputs consist of repeated tiles separated by full horizontal/vertical lattice lines. These may carry sparse exceptional colors along separators, and the output may encode only some of those exceptional values in a compact shape not equal to the number of visible panels. # ARC Grid Reasoning

Use this skill for ARC-style visual reasoning tasks where integer matrices and demonstrations define a transformation.

## Workflow

1. **Transcribe and index carefully.** Record height, width, colors, and coordinates using a consistent convention (zero-based internally is convenient). Identify background, sparse objects, repeated motifs, and candidate markers. Do not assume background solely from frequency.
2. **Compare each demo as a transformation.** Align input/output cell-by-cell. Track preserved, recolored, added, removed, or expanded cells. Check whether one local rule explains every demo, including objects near grid edges.
3. **Infer and test a compact rule.** Prefer replacement, stamping, tiling, reflection, propagation, or connecting rules over coordinate-specific descriptions. If interpretations remain ambiguous and another demo request is available, weigh its cost against the chance of a wrong submission.
4. **Establish exact template and anchor.** Record motif bounding box, orientation, anchor cell, and untouched/background cells. Determine whether marker coordinates identify the center, corner, or a particular color. Validate the offset against every demo before expansion.
5. **Construct mechanically.** Build an output matrix of exact required dimensions, then apply the rule through indexed loops or a short script. Preserve source cells when appropriate. Resolve overlapping stamps explicitly; check generated coordinates remain in bounds.
6. **Validate the actual submission.** Assert exact height and row width, integer cells 0–9, and valid JSON. Inspect changed-cell bounds and ensure the final copied action is the generated matrix, not a hand-reconstructed variant. A wrong answer with a valid grid calls for rule/alignment review; a malformed grid must first be corrected structurally.
7. **Honor the task protocol.** When exactly one action JSON is required, provide exactly that action on the last line and no extra commentary.

## Common pitfalls

- In two-panel tasks separated by a full row or column, align the panels cell-by-cell and test for intersections of their sparse foreground markers. Some outputs use a special overlap color (e.g. 3) at those intersections and fill every other output cell with the foreground color of the second panel. Infer both output colors from demos; do not assume a fixed background color across instances. Validate on every demo, because the overlap pattern may be right while the output fill color is wrong.

- For sparse same-color points, check whether the rule connects markers sharing a row or column by filling only the cells between consecutive markers with a bridge color; preserve endpoints and do not extend outside the aligned span. Validate axis separately: a demo may fill gaps only in columns (or only in rows), not both. Sort marker coordinates along each eligible line, fill only intervening cells between consecutive markers, and preserve all original markers and unrelated cells.

- A motif anchor can shift by one row or column. Write the anchor and offsets explicitly.
- A marker may be replaced by a whole multi-cell motif, not merely recolored.
- Sparse motifs may approach boundaries; validate each target coordinate before writing.
- Manually copying rows into the final action can introduce invalid row lengths even when the generated result was correct. Validate the final serialized grid.
- “Incorrect” feedback does not distinguish bad reasoning from malformed dimensions. Verify rectangularity and cell range first, then reconsider the rule.

## References

- `references/grid-validation-and-stamping.md` gives a mechanical construction and validation checklist.
